{{Short description|Norwegian physicist (1939–2019)}}
'''Gottfried Jens Feder''' (31 January 1939 – 15 February 2019) was a [[Norway|Norwegian]] physicist.

He was born in Munich, Germany but moved to live in Oslo in 1947. Following his graduation in physics, he received a NATO fellowship to study phase transitions and superconductors in Orsay, France (1965–66). He then joined [[IBM Research|IBM Zürich Research]] in Switzerland (1966–68) to study phase transitions in [[perovskites]].<ref name=obit>{{cite journal|url=https://physicstoday.scitation.org/do/10.1063/pt.6.4o.20190319a/full/|title=Gottfried Jens Feder|year=2019|journal=Physics Today|issue=3 |doi=10.1063/pt.6.4o.20190319a|access-date=3 October 2020 |last1=Aharony |first1=Amnon |last2=Jamtveit |first2=Bjørn |last3=Jøssang |first3=Torstein |last4=Malthe-Sørenssen |first4=Anders |last5=Meakin |first5=Paul |last6=Rikvold |first6=and Per Arne |article-number=22435 |bibcode=2019PhT..2019c2435. |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

He was awarded a [[dr.philos.]] degree in 1970 by the [[University of Oslo]] where, and after spending two years as a lecturer, he was appointed professor of physics, only 35 years old. His research fields were broad and varied, including condensed matter physics, fluid dynamics, complex systems, and geophysics. He cooperated closely with physicist [[Torstein Jøssang]], but also with colleagues worldwide.<ref name=snl>{{cite encyclopedia|year=|title=Jens Feder|encyclopedia=[[Store norske leksikon]]|editor=|publisher=|location=|url=http://www.snl.no/Jens_Feder|language=Norwegian|access-date=4 May 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Professor Jens Feder: Med stø hånd i fysikkfaget|last=Lippestad|first=Jenny|date=31 January 1999|work=Aftenposten|page=15|language=Norwegian}}</ref> He spent sabbaticals at the IBM T.J. Watson Research Center in Yorktown Heights, New York (1972–73), at [[General Electric Research Laboratory]] in Schenectady, New York (1978–79), as the Williams Otis Crosby lecturer of geology at MIT (1997), at the [[Isaac Newton Institute for Mathematical Sciences]] in Cambridge, UK, and at [[Imperial College London]] (1999).<ref name=obit/>

His book ''Fractals'' (Plenum, 1988) was translated into several languages, including Chinese, Japanese and Russian.<ref name=obit/>

He was elected a fellow of the [[Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters]] in 1988<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.dnva.no/c26848/artikkel/vis.html?tid=27625|title=Gruppe 2: Fysikk, astronomi, geofysikk|publisher=[[Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters]]|language=Norwegian|access-date=4 May 2014}}</ref> and a [[Fellow of the American Physical Society]] in 1989 ''"for contributions to theories and experiments on structural phase transitions and on fractals in aggregates and in porous media"''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1989&unit_id=&institution=|title=APS Fellows Archive|publisher=APS|access-date= 3 October 2020}}</ref>

He resided at [[Slemdal]] and <ref>{{cite news|title=Jubilanter|date=31 January 2014|work=Dagsavisen|page=45|language=Norwegian}}</ref>
was married to Liv Feder and they had two children.
